newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korea fires warning shot at currency speculators.
newsitem.headline: S.Korea fires warning shot at currency speculators.

text.p: South Korea's central bank on Friday warned speculators betting against the local currency, but economists said the won's slide against the dollar would not be braked.
The won has lost 3.9 percent of its value against the dollar this year after tumbling by 8.2 percent last year, mainly the result of a stubborn trade deficit.
A Bank of Korea official, who asked not to be identified, said the bank believed the currency was undervalued.
"We are ready to intervene with the same intensity as we did in February," the official said, recalling waves of dollar selling over two days last month.
His comments briefly pushed the won higher, but it ended slightly down at 879.30 after opening at 879.00.
The official vowed to hold the line at 880 won.
"If anyone goes long at the 880 level, he will risk losses," the official said.
In February, the central bank repeatedly sold dollars to defend the currency when it reached 887.00. Intervention sent the won up to 853.50 on February 20.
A tumbling won has eroded the profit margins of South Korean companies.
Yukong Ltd, the nation's largest oil refiner, saw net profit shrink to 68 billion won ($77.5 million) in 1996 from 103 billion won, due mostly to foreign exchange losses.
"We expect the dollar to rise to the 900 won level by the third quarter of this year," said Yoo Sung-hyun, a manager in Yukong's financial department.
Traders were equally sceptical the Bank of Korea could shore up the currency.

"The dollar will test 880 throughout next week," said a trader with a leading domestic bank. "Banks will temporarily retreat when the central bank steps in. But the greenback will rebound and continue its march for 900."
"The central bank changes its policy every other day," said Lee Chang-seon, an economist at LG Economic Research Institute. "No one takes the bank's comments seriously."

Meanwhile, South Koreans are protecting themselves by piling into dollars. Companies and individuals now hold around $4.4 billion in foreign currency accounts, up from $1.49 billion at the end of 1996.
Dollar selling by the central bank reduced its foreign exchange reserves to $29.8 billion at the end of February, the lowest since June 1995.
Foreigners are pulling money out of won-denominated stocks, further pressuring the local unit. In last 10 days of February, there was a net outflow of $42 million from the market.

Extra demand for dollars is also coming from commercial banks facing difficulties borrowing from Japanese counterparts, which are tightening credit lines before the end of the financial year ending in March.
Although a weaker won should help exporters and reduce the trade deficit, the effect has been spoiled because the Japanese yen has fallen even more steeply against the dollar.
